title: Colleges Want Rural Kids — But Will They Go?
summary: Picture this: you're a high school senior from a tiny town of 1,100 people. You get into one of the best colleges in the country — only 1 in 13 who apply get in! That's what happened to Jack Hancock from rural Pennsylvania. He was shocked that Amherst College even cared about students like him. Now, a big effort is underway to get more rural kids into top schools. A program called STARS, started with $20 million from a donor, has helped 90,000 rural students apply to places like Brown, MIT, and Yale. That's a 15% jump! But getting them to actually go is harder. Many rural families don't think college is worth it, or they worry about the cost. Others feel like they won't fit in with wealthier students from cities. At Amherst, they held a special visit with a campfire and s'mores to make rural students feel welcome. Jack's mom even ordered the smallest car sticker for her son's college so neighbors wouldn't think they were showing off. Colleges are learning they need to do more than just send brochures — they have to build trust.
why_it_matters: This story shows that doors can open for anyone with talent, no matter how small their hometown is, and that a little encouragement can help you take a big chance.

background_read: For a long time, many high school students from rural areas (farming or small-town places) did not apply to highly selective colleges because they thought they couldn't afford it or wouldn't fit in with wealthy city students.

Amherst College (a top private college in Massachusetts) is one of many elite schools, like Brown, MIT, and Yale, that have recently tried hard to recruit students from overlooked parts of the country.
Some wealthy donors believe that finding talented kids in small towns and helping them go to top colleges can change their lives and bring fresh perspectives to those campuses.
Article_Structure: WHO: Jack Hancock, a student from rural Pennsylvania, and the STARS program.
WHAT: Thanks to STARS, 90,000 rural students applied to elite colleges — a 15% increase — but many are still unsure they belong.
WHERE: Across the United States, particularly in small towns and farming communities.
WHY: Rural families often worry about the high cost of college and feeling out of place, so colleges are creating welcoming events to build trust.

perspectives.description: They and their families now see that top colleges might be within reach, and special campus visits like the campfire at Amherst make them feel welcome and understood.
Some still think college costs too much and worry that their children will struggle to fit in with richer students from big cities — so they don't always accept the offers.
They note that sending brochures is not enough; personal connections and building trust over time are what really convinces rural students to enroll and succeed.
